newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--US industrial output may rebound, softly.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--US industrial output may rebound, softly.

text.p: With April's strike-related slowdowns now history to the U.S. manufacturing sector, some economists believe industrial output for May could resume an upward track, Wall Street experts said.

But those gains are expected to be slight given soft consumer spending and evidence of some inventory buildup, they added. Some even forecasted another flat month of industrial production following the same in April.
"I think it will be up slightly depite the fact that man hours (in May jobs data) because of the pickup after the strike," said Robert Dederick, economist at Northern Trust.
"We're talking a slow number, and excluding automobiles it will probably be flat," he added.
The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release industrial production and capacity utilization data for May at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT on Tuesday, June 17.
Economists in a Reuters survey forecast on average industrial production rose 0.2 percent in May versus no change in April.
Capacity use, meanwhile, is expected to remain flat at 83.4 percent, the poll said.

Production was unchanged in April for the first time since last summer as strikes and related plant shutdowns at General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp took their toll, the Fed said in its April report.
Inventories may have accumulated to some degree, Dederick said, creating another possible drain on industrial production. But a low inventory-to-sales ratio means any excess inventory is very slight.
"The inventory increase is higher than one would think sustainable with the way demand has been going and chances are we'll have a mini mini inventory adjustment," he said.

Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets Inc, said an inventory buildup was "not necessarily an accident" because it appeared that manufacturers were simply accumulating inventories at a pace just strong enough to keep up with sales.

"There was an inventory buildup which may have accounted for part of that renewed strength in manufacturing early in the year but I don't think this is something unsustainable because inventories are still pretty low," Karydakis said.
Karydakis forecasts a drop in capacity utilization to 83.1 percent in May from 83.4 percent in April.
While a spike higher in production is unlikely, Dederick pointed to hefty exports and capital spending that could inflate the statistic.
Furthermore, he said news of stronger consumer spending in June may mean a rise in production is not far off.

Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Ltd economist Michael Niemira, who is looking for a 0.3 percent rise in production for May, also cited exports and capital goods as supporting growth. Computer output also continues to be strong, Niemira said.
A broad slowing down in the economy since the beginning of the year will undoubtedly be reflected in the data, he said.
The inventory problem is spotty, he said. Sectors such as apparel may be hurt given booming inventories there.

"There are selective inventory problems but presumably it's something that will work itself out over the course of the summer," Niemira said, adding that the tone of consumer spending may yet remain somewhat sluggish.
Another angle on production can be taken from recent inflation statistics, Dederick said, including Friday's reported 0.3 percent decline in the Producer Price Index for May.
But again, he added, there is no reason to believe production has surged.

"Given the inflation numbers we've been having it could be that real demand has been stronger than the nominal numbers suggest, but we've definitely have a slowing this quarter after the first quarter spree and it takes production a little while to adjust for that," Dederick said.
